section_summary: This section documents Japanese propaganda activity in the Soviet Union during the opening months of the Pacific War, including the Russian-language magazine FRONT, material circulated through the Japanese Embassy in Kuibyshev, Japan’s diplomatic justification for war, and exaggerated claims of Allied losses. It also contains late-1942 U.S. Military Intelligence reports on Japanese journalists, officers, and Russian specialists with knowledge of or experience in the Soviet Union and Manchuria. The section concludes with a 1943 cross-reference concerning Japanese engineers travelling from Kabul through Soviet territory and a 1944 charge slip.

subfiles.title: Telegram 66 reporting the Russian-language Japanese magazine FRONT
subfiles.about: Reports the confidential acquisition and intended Soviet distribution of a Japanese naval propaganda magazine titled FRONT.
subfiles.summary: Thompson describes the January 1942 inaugural issue of FRONT as a lavish, thirty-four-page Russian-language publication devoted to the Japanese Navy. He interprets its warning to anyone disturbing peace in the Orient as a threat to the Soviet Union and reports that copies were intended for selected Russians in the Far East rather than general Soviet distribution. The source requested strict protection, and Commander Allen asked that the Navy be informed.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Moscow telegram 66
subfiles.about: Paraphrases telegram 66 concerning FRONT and its apparent threat toward the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase restates that a confidential contact obtained FRONT from a Japanese Embassy employee temporarily in Moscow. It describes the magazine’s Russian text, naval imagery, military message, and restricted distribution among selected Russians in the Far East. A copy was being sent by pouch, with a request that the Navy be notified.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Chungking concerning FRONT
subfiles.about: Summarizes Thompson’s report on FRONT while emphasizing protection of the Moscow source.
subfiles.summary: The Department informs Chungking that FRONT is a January 1942 Japanese naval propaganda publication containing photographs and Russian text about Japanese military preparations. It notes an apparent threat to the Soviet Union and the planned distribution to selected Russians in the Far East. The telegram stresses that the fact that a copy was obtained in Moscow must not be disclosed.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on Japanese propaganda enclosed with despatch 1445
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese propaganda circulated in Kuibyshev and highlights Japan’s December 8 justification for war.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum inventories three items enclosed with Kuibyshev despatch 1445: Japan’s final memorandum to the United States, the Imperial Government’s war statement, and claimed American losses around Hawaii. It observes that the December 8 statement had not previously reached the Department. The document summarizes its portrayal of Japan as resisting Anglo-American tyranny and fighting for East Asian prosperity.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1445: Propaganda material distributed by the Japanese Embassy in Kuibyshev
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese Embassy propaganda obtained through the Swedish Minister in Kuibyshev.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy forwards material concerning the Pacific war that the Japanese Embassy distributed among neutral diplomatic colleagues. A member of the American Embassy staff obtained it from the Swedish Minister, who had received it with a Japanese covering note dated December 15. The enclosure was transmitted in quintuplicate.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy covering note to the Swedish Minister
subfiles.about: Encloses Japan’s final memorandum to the United States and its December 8 declaration-of-war statement.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Ambassador presents his compliments to the Swedish Minister and supplies copies of two official Japanese documents. These are the memorandum delivered by the Japanese Ambassador in Washington and the Imperial Government’s statement on war with the United States and Great Britain.

subfiles.title: Japanese memorandum terminating negotiations with the United States
subfiles.about: Presents Japan’s defense of its policies and declares further Japanese-American negotiations futile.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews negotiations since April 1941 and depicts Japan as seeking Pacific peace while the United States and Great Britain supported Chongqing, imposed economic pressure, and encircled Japan. It outlines Japan’s November 20 proposals on troop deployments, trade, oil, China, and French Indochina, then criticizes the American reply of November 26. It concludes that American principles ignored East Asian realities and that no agreement could be reached through further negotiation.

subfiles.title: Statement by the Imperial Japanese Government
subfiles.about: Justifies Japan’s declaration of war against the United States and British Empire.
subfiles.summary: The statement blames the China conflict and the Pacific crisis on resistance to Japan and on Anglo-American economic and military pressure. It claims diplomatic efforts had failed and presents war as necessary to safeguard Japan and East Asia. The declaration calls for national unity, cooperation among Japan, China, and Manchukuo, continued alliance with Germany and Italy, and construction of a Japanese-led New Order.

subfiles.title: Enemy losses in the Hawaii region by December 18, 1941
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese claims concerning American naval and air losses in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The report claims five battleships, two cruisers, and a tanker were sunk, with numerous other warships heavily damaged or repairable. It also alleges that hundreds of aircraft and multiple hangars were destroyed. The figures formed part of the Japanese propaganda package circulated in Kuibyshev.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Robert Pell concerning FRONT
subfiles.about: Suggests showing FRONT to contacts in the Coordinator of Information or its successor organization.
subfiles.summary: Henderson forwards the Japanese publication as potentially useful to American information officials. He cautions that Soviet circulation must have been extremely limited because the Japanese Embassy could approach selected high officials but could not distribute it generally. He connects the publication to Moscow telegram 66 and its reported Far Eastern audience.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary internal comment on FRONT
subfiles.about: Offers a partly illegible assessment of FRONT and its possible applicability to Russia and Western audiences.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR preserves only fragments of an internal comment addressed to Henderson. It appears to discuss the publication’s wartime message, possible relevance to Russia, racial propaganda involving the “yellow” threat, and its implications for the West. Much of the wording and the author’s identity are illegible.

subfiles.title: Despatch 14 transmitting FRONT
subfiles.from: Llewellyn E. Thompson Jr., American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of FRONT and requests strict secrecy concerning its source.
subfiles.summary: Thompson refers to telegram 66 and transmits the Japanese Russian-language propaganda magazine discussed there. He explains that the source feared being traced and asks that the magazine’s acquisition in Moscow not be divulged. The enclosure is identified as the Japanese magazine FRONT.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on Kuibyshev despatch 1494
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, drafted by Schmidt
subfiles.about: Summarizes additional Japanese naval propaganda circulated in Kuibyshev.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that despatch 1494 enclosed Russian-language propaganda obtained confidentially by an American correspondent’s secretary. The documents appeared to be letters signed by the Japanese naval attaché and listed alleged United Nations losses. Particular attention is drawn to the claim that Japan destroyed fifty-three ships assembled to evacuate Allied forces from Java.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1494: Additional propaganda material distributed in Kuibyshev
subfiles.about: Transmits English translations of further Japanese Embassy propaganda prepared in Russian.
subfiles.summary: Thurston refers to despatch 1445 and forwards additional Japanese propaganda that had received some circulation in Kuibyshev. A secretary employed by an American newspaper correspondent obtained the material confidentially and passed it to the Embassy. The translations were transmitted in quintuplicate.

subfiles.title: Japanese report on the December 8 attack in Hawaii
subfiles.about: Claims extensive American battleship, cruiser, aircraft, and shore-installation losses in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The translated letter gives purportedly photographically confirmed results of Japanese operations in the Hawaiian Islands. It claims four battleships sunk, several other warships damaged, a carrier destroyed or damaged, and hundreds of aircraft lost. It acknowledges Japanese losses of twenty-nine aircraft and five special submarines that had not returned.

subfiles.title: Japanese naval attaché’s Pacific loss report through March 7, 1942
subfiles.about: Presents statistical claims for Allied and Japanese naval, air, and merchant-shipping losses.
subfiles.summary: The letter tabulates alleged American, British, and Dutch losses from December 8, 1941 through March 7, 1942. It claims dozens of Allied warships, 1,537 aircraft, and 196 merchant ships destroyed or seriously damaged. Japanese losses are portrayed as comparatively minor, reinforcing the document’s propaganda purpose.

subfiles.title: Japanese naval attaché’s supplementary loss report
subfiles.about: Adds claims for naval losses after March 7, especially around Java and the Indian Ocean.
subfiles.summary: The attaché claims the American cruiser Marblehead and the Dutch vessel Jan van Amstel were sunk. He further alleges that Japanese forces destroyed fifty-three merchant ships gathered near Java to support Allied evacuation. Japanese losses are limited in the account to several damaged or sunk transports and lightly damaged warships.

subfiles.title: Department of State transmittal of despatch 1494
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Coordinator of Information
subfiles.about: Distributes despatch 1494 and its Japanese propaganda enclosure to U.S. intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends copies of the Kuibyshev despatch and enclosure to military, naval, and information-intelligence offices. The transmittal states that the material is being supplied in the hope that it will be of value. It identifies the enclosure as confidential despatch 1494 of March 30, 1942.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report 1014: Masao Maruyama
subfiles.from: San Francisco Office, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: Records Anatole Kolpakoff’s information about Japanese journalist and Russian-affairs specialist Masao Maruyama.
subfiles.summary: The report evaluates Kolpakoff as a reliable Russian-born source fluent in Japanese and active in U.S. broadcasts to Japan. He describes Maruyama as a journalist with perfect Russian who had represented the Tokyo-Osaka Asahi Shimbun in Moscow. Maruyama reportedly possessed motion pictures of the Kremlin and other strategic sites despite hostility toward Japanese residents in Moscow.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report 1015: Colonel Kumano
subfiles.from: San Francisco Office, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: Reports limited biographical and service information on Japanese Army officer Colonel Kumano.
subfiles.summary: Kolpakoff says he learned about Kumano chiefly through the officer’s wife, who was Colonel Akikusa’s sister. Kumano had served along the Soviet border and trained White Russian Cossacks but apparently lacked strong Russian-language skills. The report supplies his Tokyo address and cross-references an earlier report on Akikusa.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report 1017: Yoshie Nozaki
subfiles.from: San Francisco Office, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: Profiles a Japanese editor specializing in Soviet affairs and Russian-language publishing in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Kolpakoff describes Nozaki as a brilliant editor fluent in Russian and proficient in French and English. Nozaki edited Russian-language magazines and newspapers published by the South Manchuria Railway Company in Dalian and had lived in Leningrad from 1925 to 1929. His insistence on giving Kolpakoff letters of introduction to American contacts aroused the source’s suspicions.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report 1018: Masao Yonekawa, with photograph caption
subfiles.doc_type: military intelligence report with photographic enclosure
subfiles.from: San Francisco Office, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: Profiles Russian-language professor Masao Yonekawa and identifies people in an attached 1939 Tokyo group photograph.
subfiles.summary: The report identifies Yonekawa as a professor of Russian at the Imperial Military Academy in Tokyo and as a noted authority on Russian language, customs, and people. Kolpakoff describes his personality and family and notes his Japanese translations from Russian, although the surviving text breaks off. The following page captions a 1939 group photograph that includes Kolpakoff, Yonekawa and his family, Maruyama, Hishida, and the Solovehikoffs.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese engineers travelling through the Soviet Union
subfiles.about: Cross-references a telegram reporting Japanese engineers travelling from Kabul to Japan through Soviet territory.
subfiles.summary: The note states that four Japanese engineers en route from Kabul to Japan crossed the Soviet frontier on September 29. It also records a request that Moscow be informed. The original was filed under number 894.20290h/14 rather than in this subject file.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for an enclosure from file 894.20262C
subfiles.about: Records the temporary removal or transfer of an enclosure associated with another decimal file.
subfiles.summary: The page is an administrative charge slip identifying file 894.20262C and an enclosure. It bears the date January 31, 1944, clerk initials, and a largely illegible remark, but supplies no substantive account of Japanese activities.
